summary: Defines ACAP, a protocol for storing and accessing program options, configuration and preference data on a remote server. Users can then keep the same settings on different computers.

eli5.summary: It keeps your program settings on a server, so any computer you use feels the same, like a locker that follows you around.

questions: how to store application preferences on a server
what is the difference between acap and imap
subtitle: A protocol for keeping your application settings on a server so they follow you from computer to computer.

tldr.problem: Program options and preferences live on one computer, so a user who sits down at a different machine loses their settings.
tldr.mechanism: ACAP is a text protocol modelled on IMAP. A server holds a tree of datasets made of entries and attributes, with inheritance for defaults, access control lists for sharing, and SEARCH and STORE commands to read and write.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2244 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists RFC 6075 as updating it.

today: RFC 2244 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists RFC 6075 as updating it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Goals of ACAP
sections.content:
The Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP) supports remote storage and access of program option, configuration and preference information. Its main purpose is to let users reach their configuration data from multiple network-connected computers: sit down at any machine, run any ACAP-enabled application, and have your own settings.

The design favors client simplicity whenever reasonable, because the authors hope many applications will become ACAP-enabled. It is meant to be manageable, so it has inheritance for defaults, access control lists to delegate management, and quotas to control storage. A server that follows the base specification should support most future dataset classes without reconfiguration or upgrade.

It also works for clients with only intermittent access. Each entry has a server-maintained modification time so a client can detect changes, and a client can ask for the entries removed since it last connected. Because datasets may be large and links slow, ACAP offers server-side sorting, selective fetching and change notification. It is a traditional text-based Internet protocol, designed on the framework of IMAP.

By default any value may be stored in any attribute the user has permission and quota for. The server enforces validation only where a dataset class specification says so, and clients must not rely on it.
sections.eli5: The goal is simple: your settings live in one safe place on the network, so any computer can fetch them. Small changes can be fetched quickly, and nobody has to rebuild the whole thing.

sections.title: The Protocol Framework
sections.content:
ACAP assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP, and when TCP is used the server listens on port 674. It is text-based and line-oriented: lines end in CRLF, and a receiver is either reading a line or reading a counted run of octets (a literal) followed by a line.

Each client command starts with a tag, an alphanumeric identifier of no more than 32 characters, and the client SHOULD use a different tag for each command. Server data come in four forms: continuation requests (prefixed with a plus sign), completion results (OK, NO, BAD, carrying the command's tag), intermediate responses (tagged, only meaningful for a command in progress) and untagged responses (prefixed with an asterisk). A client MUST be prepared to accept any server response at any time. The client does not have to wait for one command to finish before sending another.

Data take five forms: atom, number, string, parenthesized list and NIL. Atoms are 1 to 1024 non-special characters beginning with a letter. Numbers are unsigned 32-bit values. Strings are either quoted (0 to 1024 octets) or literals, written as an octet count in braces followed by the data. A synchronizing literal makes the client wait for a + continuation before sending the data.

A server is always in one of three states: non-authenticated (where a connection starts), authenticated, or logout. If a server has an inactivity auto-logout timer it MUST be at least 30 minutes, and any command resets it.
sections.eli5: Client and server talk by passing short typed notes. Every question gets a number tag, so when answers come back in any order you know which question each one belongs to.

sections.title: Datasets, Entries and Attributes
sections.content:
An ACAP server exports a hierarchical tree of entries. Each level of the tree is a dataset, made of a list of entries. Each entry has a unique name and any number of named attributes. An attribute can be single-valued or multi-valued and carries metadata: acl, attribute, myrights, size and value. The rules for interpreting a part of the tree are called a dataset class.

Entry names are UTF-8 and cannot contain a slash. Attribute names are hierarchical, with parts separated by periods. Names without a dot are reserved for standard attributes: entry (the entry's name), modtime (last-modified time in UTC, 14 or more digits) and subdataset (a list of relative ACAP URLs locating a sub-dataset, possibly on another server).

Dataset names are a slash-separated path. The first component is the dataset class, which needs a vendor prefix or a standards-track (or IESG-approved experimental) RFC. The second is site, group, host or user, for server-wide, group, per-host and per-user data. The path /<dataset-class>/~/ abbreviates the current user's own area. Attributes are prefixed with their dataset class name, and the user. and site. subtrees are reserved for private attributes.

ACAP URLs use the form acap://server/entry, with port 674 as the default.
sections.eli5: Think of folders full of index cards. Each card has a name and a list of labeled facts on it. Folders can hold other folders, and some folders are yours, some belong to your group, and some belong to the whole site.

sections.title: Inheritance and Defaults
sections.content:
One dataset can inherit from another. The dataset it inherits from is the base dataset, and its data appears in the inheriting dataset except where a STORE has overridden it. Typically the base holds system-wide or group-wide defaults and each user has an inheriting dataset to add to or modify them.

An attribute is inherited if it was never modified by a STORE in the inheriting dataset, or if DEFAULT was stored to it. Storing DEFAULT reverts to the inherited value, while storing NIL removes the attribute. Servers MUST support at least two levels of inheritance, for example a user dataset inheriting from a group dataset that inherits from a site-wide one.

The base is named in the dataset.inherit attribute, stored in the entry with the empty name, which holds management information for the whole dataset. A SEARCH with the NOINHERIT modifier shows only the explicit overrides.
sections.eli5: The school sets default settings for everyone. You can change only the ones you care about, and if you change your mind you can say use the school's choice again.

sections.title: Searching, Contexts and Storing
sections.content:
The SEARCH command selects, sorts, fetches and monitors entries. Modifiers include DEPTH, LIMIT, HARDLIMIT, RETURN, SORT, NOINHERIT and MAKECONTEXT. Search keys such as EQUAL, PREFIX, SUBSTRING, COMPARE, AND, OR and NOT pick the entries, using named comparators. Servers MUST implement i;octet, i;ascii-casemap and i;ascii-numeric.

A context is a named subset of entries created by MAKECONTEXT. It can be enumerated (entries numbered from one, for a scrollbar-like view) and can request change notification, which arrives as untagged ADDTO, REMOVEFROM, CHANGE and MODTIME responses. A context lasts only for the session, and a server must support at least 100 active contexts. UPDATECONTEXT prods the server for pending notifications and SHOULD NOT be used for polling.

The STORE command creates, modifies or deletes entries and attributes. The server MUST make all of a single STORE's changes or none. The UNCHANGEDSINCE modifier makes a store fail with a MODIFIED response code if someone else changed the entry first, and clients writing to shared datasets are encouraged to use it. DELETEDSINCE lists entries removed since a given time so an offline client can resynchronize its cache. GETQUOTA reports a quota limit and usage in bytes.

Servers answer unknown commands with BAD. Clients MUST tolerate unknown capabilities and response codes, and new commands must be announced as a capability in the greeting.
sections.eli5: Searching is like asking the librarian for every card that matches. You can also leave a note saying tell me when a card changes, and the librarian will keep you posted. Saving is all or nothing, so you never end up with half a change.

sections.title: Authentication and Access Control
sections.content:
A connection starts in non-authenticated state, where only NOOP, LANG, LOGOUT and AUTHENTICATE are valid. AUTHENTICATE names a SASL mechanism and runs a series of server challenges and client answers. Every ACAP implementation MUST implement the CRAM-MD5 mechanism, though it MAY allow disabling it by site policy. The SASL service name is acap. Anonymous access is possible if the server supports the SASL ANONYMOUS mechanism.

Once authenticated, an access control list (ACL) decides what each user may do. An ACL is a set of identifier and rights pairs. The identifier anyone means everybody, and an identifier prefixed with a dash revokes rights. Rights from all matching identifiers are combined by taking the union of positive rights and subtracting the union of negative ones. If an attribute has no ACL, the dataset's default ACL for that attribute applies, then the dataset's default ACL, which must exist. The MYRIGHTS command tells a client its own rights.
sections.eli5: First you show your ID, in a way a snooper cannot copy. Then a list on each folder says who may look, who may write and who may change the list itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authentication, authorization, integrity and privacy come from SASL. CRAM-MD5 is susceptible to passive dictionary attacks: someone who records a session can try common passwords against it. Hard-to-guess passwords reduce this, and implementations SHOULD permit passwords of at least 64 characters. Without the optional encryption and integrity services of AUTHENTICATE or an external protection mechanism, transactions are open to passive observers and man-in-the-middle changes.

Clients that cache configuration must not let an unauthorized user read the cache; the RFC gives the example of a shared lab computer, where non-public cached data should be flushed when a user leaves. A disconnected-mode client on a laptop may wish to encrypt and password protect its cache. ACAP URLs have the same security considerations as IMAP URLs.
sections.eli5: If someone listens in on the line they might guess your password, so use a long one. And if you use a shared computer, it should forget your settings when you leave.
